maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: This is the first time a budget has been presented under Standing Order 26.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext:
Our expert on the rules, the venerable, learned and hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) points out that this is the first budget that has been presented under Standing Order 26. So. to that novelty I pay whatever tribute such a novelty deserves. But while in fairness, and one wants to be fiar, the government is rustling up some sense of urgency, its members have not ruslted up a sense of shame. They seem not really moved by the power of the terrible figures which are being visited upon the people of Canada tonight. I say that there is not really too much sensivitivy, because I have read carefully the minister's statement, and I heard it. An interesting portion was his collation of the unemployed. He said, and I quote:
No doubt the explanation is complex. Those who are recorded as unemployed include:
-men and women who have lost their regular employment;
-teenagers of age 14 or older who have decided not to return to school;
-college students who, for the time being at least, have dropped their courses;
-women who have decided to seek work;
-a large number who are seeking part-time work;
-some who are drawing unemployment insurance and some who are not;
-some who are drawing welfare benefits and some who are not. My God, he has everybody there but nonagenarians, and there are not too many of those around even in these healthy times. So it is this group, the young, the old, the people who want jobs, the people who don't want jobs, just about everybody, who comprise the unemployed. The situation has become largely like regional disparity. If the whole country is depressed you don't have to single out any one particular area. But, Mr. Speaker, I happen to come from an area that no matter how far the rest of the country depresses, our area still seems to be a little worse off because of the government which is not at the head of affairs. The Atlantic area economy is one which is used to getting the short end of the stick, used to figuring prominently in all those economic indices which are bad, and at the bottom of the list of all those that are good. We are 
growing used to that, but this does not mean that we are getting to like it.
The other day I was impressed by APEC's statement, and I understood the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) had not read the report which reads as follows:
The Atlantic Provinces Economic Council has produced a scathing indictment of the federal government's regional development efforts.
In its fifth annual review, published today, APEC assesses the 30-month record-
Thirty months, not a bad length of time.
-of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and its predecessor agencies set up by Ottawa to reduce economic disparities in Canada.
It does not call DREE a failure. But the tone of the report comes close to giving this impression-
We Maritimers are given to euphemism. We don't quite call it a failure.
The considerable degree of ministerial discretion allowed in the allocation of federal funds makes DREE susceptible to political manipulation-
Finally-and I think this is very germane to a debate such as this-the Atlantic provinces Economic Council report goes on to say:
The impact of DREE during its first years has also been reduced by national policies designed to dampen inflation.
You remember

a high degree of unemployment would be acceptable because we were going to fight inflation and drive it around the corner. It seems we are living in a circular city, because we never got inflation around the corner. The report continues:
In spite of suggestions that the region has been shielded from the full extent of these policies, APEC says the federal government's record of balancing economic policies has not been good. It believes, also, that inflation has not been halted, only postponed.
I say that when today's figures show 10.3 per cent unemployment in the Atlantic provinces, this is intolerable and not the kind of thing that any government supporter could preen himself about.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: It is 25 per cent in some areas.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext:
Yes. That is the average for the whole area, a figure which is much higher than it has been for months. I say to the government that its national policies are exacerbating the problems in the Atlantic region and that the things it is doing add to the raw unemployment figures. The government is going about the Atlantic provinces closing down operations and the very thing it should be doing something about, regional disparity, is closing down the DREE office in the Atlantic provinces. The figures nationally are bad enough, but the figures regionally are worse. I say it ill-behoves anyone to score political marks with the economy of this country in its present state.
I am sorry that I do not have any issues of the Chilliwack Progress here, but I have an issue of the Toronto Telegram and I naturally subscribe to all that is said in an article by Dr. Gillies, the dean of administrative studies at York University, one of the most eminent economists this country has ever produced. On October 12 he wrote:
October 14, 1971

Given the shocking performance of the Canadian economy in the past few years-in some respects the worst of all industrialized societies-it is not astonishing that increasing concern is being expressed about the way economic policy is formulated in Canada.
Amen!
The question is, therefore, not simply whether the Canadian political process works, but whether the particular government in power receives proper advice about economic alternatives. In short, is the system for providing economic information to the decision-makers a good one?
Thoughtful Canadians who have watched the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) come out with the most preposterous forecasts, the most far-fetched prophecies and ill-designed projections time after time, will wonder at the state of this country's economy. We would have been in a mess long ago had it not been for the fact there was a certain viability in our nation and in our people. But we have reached the stage, and every statistic is showing it, where poor government is making a poor economy and where the poor economy is injuring and weakening our nation. How long can this continue? It is a serious mess, a serious situation.
I agree profoundly with all that was said by the hon. lady from Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) who must have picked up much of her wisdom when she was married to a distinguished son of Prince Edward Island.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext:
She was correct in her appraisal of what the government is doing. However, I am not going to traverse ground which was well covered by my colleagues tonight. Another thing that fascinated me about the Minister's statement tonight was his closing paragraph:
Mr. Speaker, the economy is strong and growing. The measures I have proposed today are designed to keep it that way.
Anybody who can say that can belong to a government which says the Americans do not understand our problems. How can anyone in the United States or anywhere else believe in the credibility of the Minister of Finance? The very night, when unemployment is at its worst in over a decade, he stands up without a smile on his face, without a joke on his lips and says the economy is strong and growing. He is a glaring example of his own incredibility, and I hope that incredibility will lead to his departure from the job in which he has given an incredible performance.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you may
well understand, I could not remain silent in the wake of the statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) in view of the prevailing economic situation.
I had the privilege of listening closely to the statement of the Minister of Finance as well as to the succeeding speeches of the leaders of the opposition parties. I must admit very objectively that those leaders made very valid criticisms. I must also acknowledge the seriousness of the economic situation, and I think that it was urgent for the government to make those statements and also that it is our responsibility to seek solutions in order to improve the lot of the Canadian people.
The Canadian Economy
I shall not dwell any longer on unemployment statistics. They have been dealt with often enough. We are all aware of the fact that unemployment plagues our economy. Our Canadian economy is in jeopardy, regardless of what the minister may say. He has insisted it is "strong", that it will continue to be so. He was perhaps verging on exaggeration.
On the other hand, I must recognize, in view of the statements of the Minister of Finance and the commitments made by the government tonight, that the government deserves praise for its efforts.
One can always say it is too little and too late. Yet, it must be recognized that large amounts of money will be spent on improving the difficult situation we are now witnessing.
I am always happy to see someone trying.
In the circumstances, I am of course gratified by the statement made by the Minister of Finance. It would be quite simple to repeat, as so many others have done, that the measure unfortunately comes too late. I must still admit that opposition party leaders, among them the leader of the Progressive Conservative party (Mr. Stanfield) and the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Lewis) have brought forward excellent suggestions and well-founded criticisms.
I must also recognize that for several months party leaders have been recommending that funds be allocated to remedy the prevailing situation.
I believe party leaders were not wrong to express their criticisms and that the Minister of Finance has also shown wisdom by announcing the measures which I hope will be likely to improve the situation. Will it be enough? Only somebody with the gift of second sight can answer that.
I keep turning back to the thought that since effort is always rewarded, I should rejoice when people attempt to improve a really complex situation.
I feel that we have been looking for a long time for some instant solution which would ensure greater well-being for the whole Canadian community. Such an easy answer would be rather surprising.
I met recently with a number of my constituents in order to discuss the needs of my constituency, as well as the present economic situation. I have had occasion, in the past year or so, to suggest to the government that it consider introducing a policy designed to lower to 60 the age of eligibility for old age security pension.
I know that the remarks I have already made certainly have not been noticed by the government as much as I would have wished. Indeed I had discussions with enough constituents of mine to ascertain the merits of that idea and, after having got certain figures which proved that from 350,000 to 400,000 workers were between 60 and 65,1 think the government was wrong in seeking the instant solution. Some political parties have perhaps forgotten that there is a simple solution, one which is perhaps too simple to be valid, but I remain convinced that we must consider the possibility of giving the old age security pension to people of 60 and tonight I would like to take the opportunity to submit that proposal to the government.
8726

October 14, 1971
The Canadian Economy
In my opinion it would be very easy to reduce unemployment by about 70 per cent. But several millions of dollars will be spent to try to implement the proposals made by the Minister of Finance. I fully agree that the government should make all possible efforts and have millions of dollars available, but I wonder if the problem should not be dealt with more seriously by considering the possibility of granting the old age security pension to people of 60.
When referring to a policy liable to create from 350,000 to 400,000 jobs for young people, which would enable them to earn a living and take advantage of a well-deserved retirement at 60 after 30 or 40 years of service, we must at the same time consider the possibility of increasing old age pensions.
Some hon. members may say that I have talked about this policy before. It is not an innovation, nor an invention, but I do intend, as I said a few weeks ago, to repeat it as long as the government will not give it sufficient consideration.
Since this policy could create a social climate much more acceptable than the one we are experiencing today,-I believe it is up to the government to apply it. An old age security policy to provide the first payment at 60 would help to create between 350,000 and 400,000 jobs for the young people who are waiting and costing the government so much. I am wondering if it would not be desirable to take this proposal into consideration due to the importance of this debate. As a matter of fact, this solution would not require an enormous amount of money, since the cost of the 700,000 unemployed is extremely high. Must we repeat that it would be a transfer to allow people 60 years of age to have an income of at least $100 a week?
We did not hesitate to vote for the new unemployment insurance program providing benefits of up to $100 a week. We know full well that several people receive welfare benefits of more than $100 a week and I still cannot understand why the government would not consider the possibility of giving people 60 years of age well deserved vacations, thus reducing the present unemployment by 70 per cent.
Perhaps we shall have to admit that it is not easy to put aside 350,000 to 400,000 workers? Must we ask the government to envisage, for instance, a voluntary pension, a voluntary old age security program for the next six months by making payments of $100 a week to those pensioners? We could find in less than six months 200,000 persons at least who would be interested in leaving their job, since they would be sure of getting a sufficient income. People, 60 and over, would thus continue to be an asset to society since their income would be enough to allow them to take those trips they dreamed about for so long and to live decently.
And in the next six months, let us suppose that such a pension will necessarily be granted to people of 60 thus curing in 12 months this disease called unemployment which is hurting so unfairly the Canadian economy while creating an unfavourable social climate.
I take it upon myself to repeat this request to the government but considering the efforts it has made over the last two years I am not among those who would take this opportunity simply to blame the government saying that it

has not done anything. We know very well that for a year and a half now the government has, for instance, spent millions in order to improve the situation. However, one must admit that the expected success has not materialized. I wonder to what extent those responsible in this government are ready to admit that they have not succeeded in providing the better standard of living and the stability that all Canadians and both opposition and government members want.
I take this opportunity to invite the government to consider seriously the possibility of granting the old age security pension at age 60, because, in my view, that would be the least costly solution as we would be providing work for 350,000 to 400,000 persons who cost a great deal to the government. We could also raise the amount of the old age pension, as this is necessary would ensure a sufficient income to those people aged 60 and over. That would give new hope to the young who are waiting for jobs. They are disappointed, and this creates a difficult social climate in Canada.
Events that occurred last year surely demonstrate that the government should hasten to do something which would represent a true solution. Statements by the Minister of Finance tonight were in good faith, and I support them, I am pleased with them, but I wonder just how much they are seeking this cure-all solution that no one, I think, has in this Chamber. It does seem that they have not succeeded in finding a proper solution.
I would therefore restrict myself to a few comments in the hope that the government will consider suggesting a solution. I was expecting tonight that the Minister of Finance would in his speech refer to this policy which I have at heart, because of the opportunity I have had of talking with people in this age group and I know how happy they would be if they were to retire at the age of 60, provided they are assured to obtain from the government the bare necessities of life.
In addition to all the suggestions made by the minister involving several millions of dollars, I dare hope that far greater and far more serious consideration will be given to the housing problem.
I think that the statement mentioned $113 million to be divided among the ten provinces. This is more or less important, but how many hon. members would like to see the 11 per cent tax on building materials eliminated? What mattered was not so much making available millions of dollars for excessive loans to middle-income people. One must recognize that a growth in the building industry would bring about a solution to unemployment. That could be made possible with better loans, an extension of the reimbursement period, as long as the interest rates remain at the same level.
How many hon. members have suggested that the tax on building materials should be eliminated? I for one had the pleasure of making such a recommendation. All those interested in this matter should get together with the government and set up a true policy which would restart the building industry and give work to thousands of unemployed. The government should meet those people immediately.
October 14, 1971

I was happy to learn today that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) have decided to meet with spokesmen for certain unions and a certain group of businessmen. A few weeks ago during the debate on Bill C-262, I had the opportunity of requesting a summit meeting, acknowledging that nobody had miracle solutions. I asked the government to arrange a conference with unions, management, economists, businessmen and industrialists so that they would join their efforts to find a solution which might be the best one under the circumstances, and admitting that the economy is in a bad predicament.
I would not dare saddle the government with the sole responsibility for our current economic situation. However, I must acknowledge that since we have not found that miracle solution everybody is looking for, it might be possible to find an acceptable solution by following the advice of experienced businessmen, after agreements with employee and employer unions. This would be a way of bringing home to the public, to those unions or organizations that it is important to join hands to try and find a global solution rather than being satisfied with criticizing the government and, especially, rejoicing over the difficulties that it is now experiencing.
I have listened carefully to the speech of the Minister of Finance and I was disappointed to see that some hon. members were happy to witness the problems the government is facing, whereas we know very well the price the Canadian people will have to pay to get them settled. We might do well-I must repeat it-to ask the members of the House to suggest interesting solutions that the government could keep in mind in order to provide for the well-being of people and iron out present difficulties.
I must recognize that certain opposition members and even some of their leaders, recommended the reduction in personal income tax a few months ago. Now the government does just that. As some people criticized the government for it, the delay was a costly one, but I nevertheless recognize that the government realized the situation and is making efforts to deal with it.
I also recognize that projections made a few months ago were refuted by events. I believe now the government should not be ashamed of recognizing that some projections were wrong and that they surely need better qualified economic advisers.
I should not like to deprive other members of the opportunity to speak. I will limit myself to those few comments, in the hope, in the event I did not shed any light-I am not qualified for that-of at least having made suggestions worthy of greater attention on the part of the government.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am indeed pleased to take part in this debate. I consider this a very important matter and one of great concern. In particular, it is of great concern to the riding that I represent. We have a great deal of unemployment in my riding. Many people who live and work there are now out of a job. We have great concern about this. It is a riding where the United States surcharge is affecting manufacturing and industry in general to a great extent. It is a riding where there is a great deal of uncertainty about the future. We have a great deal of concern for
The Canadian Economy
these people. It is a riding where businesses and corporations have been phasing out because of circumstances over which they have no control.
I represent these working people. I have concern for them. The party of which I am a member also has concern for them. As a matter of fact, the Liberal party of Canada has always been known as the workingman's party.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: That is true, in spite of what members of the New Democratic Party may say. They may represent the big unions but they do not represent the working people.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext:
This government has concern for the people. It wants to help people, reduce unemployment, provide jobs and curtail inflation. For two years we have been trying to do this through the Prices and Incomes Commission which has been successful in part with their voluntary restraints. They received support from every sector except the New Democratic Party and the big unions.
What did the members of the NDP say? They said, "No, we are not going to support Canadians in this venture- not one bit. We want everything we can get out of the economy and we are going to take it. We do not care who suffers." Even though this may be at the expense of the unorganized, the pensioners, widows and orphans, they could not care less. They want to have their cake and eat it too.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: There is no cake with Trudeau.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext:
This is a flexible government. It is flexible to changes in the economy and changes in society. It is ready, willing and able to make tough decisions. It made a tough decision today when it in effect pumped $1 billion into the economy.
I was disappointed with the approach taken by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). His whole attitude was one of "I told you so." He did not have anything constructive to say. He made no suggestions, only destructive criticism. One can have nothing but contempt for this kind of approach. What did the leader of the New Democratic Party have to say? It was the usual gloom and doom approach of too little, too late. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that $1 billion is a great deal of money to be considered as too little.
This government realizes the time has come to prime the economic pump, and you don't do that with a thimbleful of water; you use a whole pailful if you want results. That is what the government is doing. The government means business. It prefers to take action and take it effectively.
The leader of the New Democratic Party talked about the 7 per cent corporate tax cut. He seemed to think this was a terrible thing. In effect, he said it discriminates against private individuals who receive an income tax cut of 3 per cent. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, where do the jobs come from? Who creates the jobs? The NDP cannot fool

October 14, 1971
The Canadian Economy
the people into thinking they create the jobs. The people know that jobs are created by industry. They are not taken in by the hypocrisy of the NDP and its philosophy. We want to prime the economy and that is exactly what we are doing. I believe the steps taken will prove effective. We want jobs.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: For whom?

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext:
We want to create as many as possible in the labour sector. That is exactly what we are doing. I should like to compliment the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) for his thoughtful in-depth approach to stimulating all sectors of the economy. I would say that $1,070 million will provide economic stimulation. It certainly is not any band-aid approach. In effect, it is a complete bandage. Added to the $80 million we approved the other day, it will certainly give confidence to the business community, stimulate the economy and create more jobs. The program outlined by the minister is far-reaching and objective. It is no death-bed repentance of Benson as has been suggested. On the contrary, it illustrates the determination of the government to resolve the fiscal and economic difficulties brought about by the United States surcharge and other factors.
The program is imaginative and diversified. It provides for immediate relief projects as well as for long-term benefits. It provides help to municipalities and provinces. It helps industry and business. It helps the untrained worker, the trained worker and the unemployed. It provides for on-the-job training, a new concept to help the worker in this changing technological age. The government takes cognizance of the fact that we live in a changing world, a changing society. We live in a society with changing values, in a complete era of change. This government is heedful of change when change is needed. It is also capable of making big decisions when big decisions are needed. I am sure the big decision made today to stimulate the economy with $1 billion will stimulate the economy to the benefit of all Canadians.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have just heard a very interesting speech from the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson), one which will certainly well qualify him to be No. 28 on the list of parliamentary secretaries, whatever the precise figure may be. You can always live in hope, just like the unemployed in this country.
The hon. member said the government was not taking a band-aid approach when it brought forward this program of economic stimulation tonight. I agree with him. It is not a band-aid approach. But, unfortunately for the people of Canada, they have just about bled to death before the government could find anything to put on the wound. That is the sad thing. One has to look at the situation today and compare it with the situation three and a half years ago when the government went to the people of Canada and talked about a just society, talked about the elimination of regional economic disparity, talked about streamlining Parliament, talked about doing all the things that were great and wonderful for the Canadian people. And the Canadian people bought it.
What did the government do? First of all, they came back and streamlined Parliament. They took almost all

the power away that the opposition has possessed in the past, so there was no problem left for the government in passing the legislation that it is desired to pass.
The next thing we found happening was that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was manufacturing a super bureaucracy, a bureaucracy that has now grown to the point that he has 81 people on his personal staff, according to the last answer I received on the subject, at a total cost in excess of $800,000 to the Canadian taxpayer, and that the Privy Council Office had a staff of 206 people at last count at a total cost of in excess of $2.5 million annually to the Canadian taxpayer. The technocrats were put together. The super bureaucrats were put together. They were going to produce a new and vital type of government which was going to solve all the problems faced by the Canadian people.
What do we find today? We find ourselves in a position where we have the highest unemployment rate in a decade. We find ourselves in a position where a government, which a year ago was creating unemployment, now does not know how to stop it from continuously snowballing and snowballing to a point where we can very easily have three quarter of a million to a million unemployed before the winter is over. They deliberately created it.
I was pleased to listen to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) speaking tonight. Tonight, the minister condemned the policy that last year he said was courageous when the Prime Minister said we could live with an unemployment rate of 6 per cent. He said: Never again will the government endeavour to create unemployment to combat inflation. We knew what it was like to face a recession, because when we became the government in 1957 we inherited a recession. We knew how hard it was to stimulate the economy. We told them not to put the brakes on because if they did it they would get themselves into a situation from which they could not extricate themselves. Now, we find that the government has to pump over $1 billion into the economy in the hope of alleviating what is snowballing into probably the worst economic recession since the dirty 'thirties.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: Depression.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext:
Recession, depression, it does not really make any difference what you call it. For a great many people in this country it means nothing but misery and suffering. With this tremendous staff the Prime Minister has around him one would have thought that before now we could have had something original in the way of programs to stimulate the economy. When one examines what this government is proposing, one finds it is exactly what the Diefenbaker administration used between 1957 and 1961 to stimulate the economy. Dress it up any way you want, it is exactly the same thing. But the sad fact is that these proposals should have been put into effect last April, not today-certainly at the latest last June when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) brought down his budget.
We have now reached a point in this Parliament where the credibility gap of the Minister of Finance is wider and deeper than the Grand Canyon. There is no way that any Canadian can put faith any longer in what the Minister
October 14, 1971

says. His usefulness as a member of the executive has been spent. As a matter of fact, it was spent a long time ago. The only way this government can hope to revive any of its credibility is to have a cabinet shuffle and remove the Minister of Finance at the earliest possible moment. I hope that when the Prime Minister holds his press conference tomorrow he will tell the Canadian people that the government of this country is going to have a new Minister of Finance. As a matter of fact, if he told us we were going to have no Minister of Finance we would be better off than keeping the present one.
Yesterday I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) whether he would use some of the 287 people he has on his staff to re-examine the policies under DREE, to see whether there was not a better way of implementing programs that would assist in eliminating economic disparity which has now spread across the whole nation. No longer is it unique to the maritime provinces and parts of Quebec; it is everywhere in Canada. The Prime Minister replied to me, "Well, I will speak with the President of the Treasury Board and see if I can get some more staff". No doubt the Prime Minister was trying to be sarcastic and was inferring that I was asking questions about his staff.
I think the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean) made the best suggestion. He suggested it would be of value if the Prime Minister were willing to add at least two people to his staff-a psychologist to help him understand. what is going on in the world and a psychiatrist to help him understand what his government is doing. Even if this cost the taxpayer another $40,000 it would probably be a good idea to take on this extra staff. Then, hopefully, we would get some programs and proposals that would benefit the unemployed of this nation.
Looking at some of the proposals that have been made, I note that among other things the government is providing $100 million for projects to be developed through municipal and community organizations. I wonder what type of program this is going to be. I would hate to think that this winter we are to have a repetition of the Opportunities for Youth program of this summer. I think that as much as the Canadian public wants to see unemployment alleviated and the government go to almost any length to achieve that end, it would rather see something better than the screwball schemes that were incorporated in the Opportunities for Youth program this summer which brought discredit to our young people, many of whom were enthusiastic, dedicated and objective in their ideas. I hope there will be a better type of screening apparatus set up by the government regarding the proposals that will be coming forth from community organizations as to winter works projects.
No one objects to the pump-priming the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) talked about. But we do object to the fact that these proposals are made now rather than last April, May or June at a time when provincial and municipal governments would have been able to dovetail their programs with the federal scheme, thereby allowing for a concerted effort to meet the high rate of unemployment which today is very much in evidence in every province.
We are now in the position where many of the programs that are being undertaken will not effectively come into operation until next spring. The fact is that the unem-
The Canadian Economy
ployed will be unemployed all winter whether or not the government endeavours to do anything about it. This is a pretty sad situation for many people. Many of the unemployed already have been unemployed for four months and they face another three or four months before they have any hope of there being employment opportunities.
The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) displayed his knowledge of urban affairs in an excellent contribution this evening. He pointed out the great dilemma of the big cities of Canada in the field of welfare and asked where they will get the money to pay welfare to people who require it during the winter. All welfare budgets in the big cities have, in the minds of the financiers, gone beyond all comprehension. They do not know where to find the money they require. They cannot go to their taxpayers for more. I hope that some of the $1,070 million that is to be pumped into the economy will find its way into the treasuries of the municipalities of the nation to assist them to meet welfare payments which they are forced to make to people who cannot find work even if they want to work, as most of them do.
I think the best way to describe this government is that it is one that swallows itself. It said one thing yesterday, and this evening it goes off in the opposite direction. We are happy to see it go in the opposite direction because certainly its former policies were going in the wrong direction. In fact, we are not sure that the government is even competent to implement the policies and programs it is proposing.
I should like to take a moment to describe a situation that very clearly indicates just how two-faced this government has been, and compare yesterday with today. Among many of the things that are described as ways and means of combating inflation is a much broadened manpower program.
On April 30, I received a reply to a letter that I wrote to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) on March 19. In that letter I asked the minister to assist me in increasing the size of an upgrading school in the town of Amherst sponsored by Manpower. I wanted it doubled in size because I knew there were many people who required upgrading in my constituency, who desired it, and who would then be in a position to take vocational training and then enter the labour market. This would not do them much good now, but at least they would be qualified. I asked the minister for his assistance. He explained to me in a long letter why this could not be done. He said, in effect, that in November 1970 additional funds became available for the training of the unemployed in the winter months, and another 15 trainees were referred to training. They terminated their courses on March 26, 1971. He said: As this program is now terminated, the number of trainees is again based on regular allocations and presently 45 students are attending upgrading courses.
In other words, there was no way in which I was going to obtain any more money from the manpower program to assist the unemployed who wanted upgrading.
The situation in the town of Springhill was exactly the same. The member of the legislature for Cumberland Centre wrote me enclosing a letter from the Springhill Chamber of Commerce. They wanted an upgrading

October 14, 1971
The Canadian Economy
course established in the town of Springhill similar to that which existed in Amherst. This is what the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang) wrote to Mr. Raymond M. Smith, M.L.A., and to William B. Harroun, secretary of the Springhill Chamber of Commerce. The letter is dated May 27 and it reads:
This is further to my departmental Assistant's letter of May 7, 1971 about occupational training in the town of Springhill.
At the present time a basic training for skill development school with a capacity of 45 trainees is operating in Amherst. A large proportion of the trainees at Amherst are from Springhill. There is a backlog of clients for the basic training for skill development course in both Springhill and Amherst and they will be provided with training as quickly as possible. However, it is not possible to establish facilities to accommodate all those requiring training at the same time.
Some training is being provided at the Cumberland County Regional Vocational School in Springhill on a second-shift basis. Officials of the department will discuss with the province the possibility of increasing the training offered at this school. It is not considered desirable at this time to recommend to the province that additional training facilities be established at Springhill. It is felt that the Amherst school will be able to adequately service the area.
Maybe now at this late date the Minister of Manpower and Immigration will reconsider his decision.
I want to put this second letter on the record as well because it comes from the minister's departmental assistant. It is about one of the many people who were trying to secure this training. This is what it said:
This is further to my letter of August 10, 1971, concerning Mrs. (Geraldine) Babineau (Rushton) Springhill, Nova Scotia.
The report I have received from the Amherst Canada Manpower Centre indicates that the number of persons who wish to take basic training courses in Springhill is much greater than the number of training places made available. In such circumstances, it becomes necessary to establish a stand-by list of those persons who cannot be referred to training as soon as they register.
Mrs. Babineau's name is entered on such a list at the Springhill Canada Manpower Centre and she will be notified as soon as a training place becomes available. Regretfully it is not possible to state a specific date on which a course will be available to her.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but I do so to advise him that his time has expired.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to say a few words about the economic situation, the government's projects and the conditions to their implementation.
The government has been made aware of the economic conditions. It decided to act against unemployment increase, to react to distressed requests, cost of living increase and economic imbalance. All those things made the government respond in the proper manner.
I do not want to take too long at this late hour. I shall go straight to the point. I would not like to repeat what the previous speakers said, because so many things were said. Figures were given; I shall not go over them.
The economic stagnation will get worse. We will lighten the tax burden insofar as we will let this government accumulate huge deficits and let our institutions go heavily into debt and pay exorbitant interest rates to big business.
But never, in this chamber, did those responsible put the finger on the real economic ailment. The economic situation will go from bad to worse; we will have to spend billions, which will create awful deficits at all levels of government, especially for the federal government.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) says that we will accumulate in 1973 a deficit of $2.6 billion, whereas we already have one of $1 billion for this year. And in 1972, we will have one of $2,600,000,000, with all the programs and all the tax exemptions that are being granted to the people. To enable the people to breathe a little, increased deficits will be allowed. Through those conditions alone, we will succeed in balancing the economy. The economy will become more and more unbalanced and those programs, tax increases, higher debts and increased deficits will never foster a balance of the economy.
The people will never be satisfied in this wealthy country. We could profit therefrom, provided that we drive the Canadian people to the wall. When some advantages are granted to Canadians, the time comes where they must be removed, after some relaxation of the economy. It is then necessary to impose restrictions on credit and to increase taxes to again balance the budget.
I warn the government: the economic measures taken today will not last long and we will accumulate frightful debts we will be unable to pay. I must tell the Canadian people they will not enjoy for long the advantages of this policy which it is claimed will save everyone.
To hear the economists and politicians talk, and in particular the Minister of Finance, the entire Canadian society has been pulled out of stagnation, is once more on a stable footing. That is nothing but sham; that is a lie. On the contrary: the Canadian people are being plunged into appalling stagnation which will have disastrous consequence within a few months.
When a new government comes to power, it will be said logically that it will have to balance its budget. A government that has a deficit and that unbalances the taxpayers' budget to balance its own, establishes an unbalanced system, which has no reason for being, and those who accept this are totally wrong. This error will continue if those salvaging bodies, the benefits of which are acclaimed today, are maintained.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people, those who do not understand our economy, who do not know where we are going, who are not aware of our responsibilities and of the consequences of the actions taken, believe that this makes sense. There are even members here who in my opinion are not aware of the consequences that that will bring about. As a matter of fact, that will not settle in any way the prevailing unbalanced economic problem.
Mr. Speaker. I would urge the government to bring in real social measures, to lower the cost of living. I would ask them to reduce taxes, to decrease interest rates, to issue new credit without interest in order to cure the present economic uneasiness. That would be real social measures, real economic measures, real measures designed to balance our outmoded economic system. It is completely off balance and those measures will never balance our unbalanced economy.
(Mr. Coates.]
October 14, 1971

Mr. Speaker, I will not go any farther tonight, because I think that I have said enough.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have been listening to a lengthy dissertation about the economic problems which face Canada. Tonight, we saw the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) come out with a budget which cannot really be answered in a normal and formal budget debate. That is perhaps why we still find ourselves here debating the pros and cons of the economy, and the worth and strength of the measures proposed by the Minister of Finance.
Many people have said that the minister is reducing personal income tax by 3 per cent and corporation tax by 7 per cent, providing $340 million for municipal projects in something like a modern winter works program, and coupled with this, job retraining. To really understand Canada's economic plight one can quote the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) who said something to the effect that never again should any government try-I wrote down what he said-to control inflation by fiscal and monetary measures which bring about high unemployment. We all well remember the Prime Minister's famous statement that he did not care if he brought about 6 per cent unemployment, that he could live with it, and the people could either take it or lump it. He was going to cure or control inflation.
But in studying the economy one has to take a quick look at what really did happen. From 1965 to 1968, Canada had the highest rate of inflation in the western world. The Prime Minister then took over and he became obsessed with the idea of curing inflation. On several occasions, the Minister of Finance boasted that from 1968 to 1970 Canada had the lowest rate of inflation. So, we were experimenting, and I agree with the Minister of Labour that never again should a government use a cruel, blunt tool in such a fashion as to bring about unemployment.
Finally on May 30, 1970, the Minister of Finance had to float the Canadian dollar because he, too, had been obsessed with the idea of stopping inflation, and he found there was just too much pressure on the Canadian dollar. This came about partly because the white paper on tax reform frightened the economic community in Canada. Has the confidence of the economic sector been restored? That is the question we really have to ask ourselves. Up until tonight, it certainly has not been restored. We would like to think that it can be restored, but when one hears about the Gray Report, and what the government is going to do to foreign corporations and foreign investment in Canada, one wonders. We do not know whether that report is shelved or written into Bill C-259. I believe a lot of it is written into Bill C-259. That bill still has the economic community of Canada somewhat worried.
We have been through what might be called an exercise in tax reform that has lasted between eight to ten years. The country has become worried about it. The tax reform bill is 700 pages long. Yesterday, the Minister of Finance filed 100 amendments. Now today, before we have even finished study of clause 1 in committee of the whole, the minister brings in a budget of quite mammoth size, turning loose over $1 billion more in our economy. But all the
The Canadian Economy
while the very tax legislation that we are going to study is going to increase taxes by $850 million.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: That is sheer nonsense, and you know it.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext:
The hon. parliamentary secretary must have just wakened, Mr. Speaker. In any case, the business community has not got confidence in the Canadian government. It is worried and frightened. Its members look ahead, as did Mr. Filion in his speech in Quebec not so long ago. He asked what do we see? We see the American surtax, and this government trying to get into a trade war. Apparently, we are going to use all our options.
That reminds me of a former premier of Alberta who did not call an election for June. He said he was keeping all his options open. In fact, he was closing his options, and in fact that is what the government is doing with regard to the American surtax measure. Members of the government brought it on themselves, and it is too bad the Canadian economy will have to suffer because of their thoughtless action.
In January, 1970, the Prime Minister made his famous statement about 6 per cent unemployment. Tonight, he went out of the House of Commons laughing, and said to the Minister of Labour, "Bryce, you had better look after it; you won't need any help." Then, he went out laughing about 7.1 per cent unemployment and the measures which the Minister of Finance hopes will be of benefit. The 7 per cent reduction in corporation tax will not be immediately felt in the economy. In fact, it may take some time before it is ploughed back into business, into job creation, because of the loss of confidence in the Canadian government shown by the business community.
Money today is leaving Canada. It is not a question of foreign investment in Canada anymore. We are now in a position where money is leaving Canada. Canadians are looking for a place more secure than Canada in which to invest their money. In a country so rich in natural resources that, to me, is nearly a sin. It is because people have lost confidence. They are looking ahead and they see the labour code introduced by the Minister of Labour. The labour code bill introduced by the Minister of Labour is frightening business. Now the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) has introduced a competition bill, which also frightens business, a bill under which he is going to set up a seven man tribunal, appointed for ten years, answering to nobody, ruling authoritatively on both sides of a question, dealing with business amalgamatioris, foreign investment, and the whole role of Canadian corporations in Canada. I do not believe this will really benefit the unemployed.
The Minister of Finance can come out with all the job retraining programs he likes, and with all the municipal programs he likes. After a while people will be retrained, but there will be no use in being retrained if there are no jobs. There will be no jobs unless the country grapples with the fact that the business community has to have confidence in the government. The government has to pay attention to the country and show some concern and interest. This government has failed to do that.
Just last week we were debating whether the government should pay the $60 million to the farmers. If they

October 14, 1971
The Canadian Economy
had wanted to establish an acreage payment program, the bill might have gone through. The Minister of Finance said the farmers could not have it both ways. He said, "You take the $60 million or the $100 million; we haven't got the money". All of a sudden the government has a billion dollars when last week they did not have $60 million. In order to manage a society and in order to manage an economy, you have to be sensitive to every little condition that may arise in every region. You cannot operate as insensitively as the Minister of Finance or the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) with his cold, callous attitude toward many Canadians. You must be concerned.
Two years ago the government should have primed the pump. There are few people on the government side in the House of Commons who know anything about pumppriming and pumping water. Once the water stops flowing it sometimes takes a prime to get it going again. The government shut off the pump.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: Sheer nonsense!

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext:
It is always nonsense to the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Mahoney) who is so knowledgeable. He has an air of arrogance, but I know deep down he really is not.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) said that the unemployment rate is no higher than it was in the sixties. But we had the Governor of the Bank of Canada controlling the money supply in 1960 and part of 1961. Our money supply did not increase at all, it shrank. We had high unemployment because there was no money in the economy.
The Minister of Finance admitted that the money supply is growing at a faster rate than ever before. In other words, they are creating money to cut down on the number of unemployed. But when the community into which the money is poured has no confidence in the business climate created by this government, the money is of no real use. That is why we have over 7 per cent unemployment today. The government has destroyed the confidence of the country.
In his speech the Minister of Labour said that everybody should be afraid the NDP is going to take over and things would be worse. I am not afraid of the NDP or their philosophy-how can it be worse?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: At least they have a chance.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: How can it be worse when you have a government that is not interested in the country or the people?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: You have no alternative.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext:
Now, we have this very nice person from Calgary South with so much knowledge expressing an opinion which again shows that he must be a very arrogant person. I know he is not, but he gives that impression and I wish he did not. My constituency borders his and I would like to think that we can be compatible some of the time.
The economy is in a poor state today because the government has deliberately destroyed confidence in the business world. Somehow or other more interest must be shown in Canada and what affects the economy. When

this is done maybe some confidence will return and we will see a reduction in unemployment next summer. I noticed that the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Finance would make no predictions for this winter. The Minister of Labour suggested that savings are at an alltime high. They are, and people are not reinvesting. The white paper on taxation started this fear in the business community and the attitudes of the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister contributed to it, as did the Competition Act and a number of other things.

speechtext:
I would like to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that when the hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Pringle) and the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) referred to the Prices and Incomes Commission it seemed strange that the Minister of Labour and his parliamentary secretary were not applauding. Those members blamed the labour movement for not being involved with the Prices and Incomes Commission. Anyone who has looked into the situation realizes that the labour movement was prepared to go along with the commission if it had added the third ingredient, profits, and if it had added dividends and interest rates. But the commission had only two ideas, prices and incomes. The other things did not matter.
I was very surprised that the hon. member for Fraser Valley East and the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore, who pretend to be supporters of the workers of this country, would attack these people as they have tonight. I believe they should look into the record when they compare the labour movement in Canada to that in the United States. They suggested that the labour movement in Canada was not prepared to co-operate in an effort to stabilize the various aspects of the economy that affect every person in this country.
I have heard considerable talk tonight, Mr. Speaker, about generating money and jobs. We have had considerable debate in this House for the last two weeks concerning the prairie agricultural economy. We heard tonight that if so many millions of dollars are put into the economy it will generate jobs and provide an uplift for the economy generally. I suggest that if the sums the government now talks of had been made available earlier, if the government had paid out $100 million under the so-called acreage payments, if it had paid out the $95 million owing to the farmers under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act, and if it had paid out the $70 million that ought to have been available under a two-price system for wheat, $1 billion would have been put into the economy. That would have created many jobs for manufacturing industries in central Canada and would have brought untold benefits to the Canadian economy.
Somehow we are hung up with the idea that money put into the western economy does not generate many job opportunities elsewhere. I suggest that the economy of
October 14, 1971

western Canada is as important as that of central Canada and the economy of eastern Canada, in exactly the same way, is important to the economy of central Canada.
I think we have all heard of the local opportunities programs. I read about it two or three weeks ago in one of the editions of Labour News. It is said that local opportunities programs will be initiated and that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang) will probably have jurisdiction over them. I think the kindest thing we could do to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration is unload from his shoulders some of the jobs that he now has.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: There we have lost opportunities.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext:
I suggest that the present load the minister is carrying is big for him. We know what has happened so far as Manpower is concerned. We know that in many cases people cannot undertake more than 52 weeks training at one time. In some instances they must wait before undertaking another period of retraining. Some people do this for three years. Some people who have been able to continue training under manpower training programs for up to two years have tried to get a few extra weeks' training but have been told that no money is available. Tonight we heard that extra money is to be made available for the retraining of people. I think the minister will agree that such manpower programs are needed and that they will bring about the results we all desire.
In addition to these responsibilities the minister also answers in this House for the Canadian Wheat Board. That alone is a full-time job. It is passing strange that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) does not have responsibility for the Canadian Wheat Board. It seems to me that the minister is on the chopping block and that they are trying to spread one minister around too far. He cannot possibly do an adequate and satisfactory job in the many areas for which he has responsibility.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: He is expendable.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext:
All members of the House know that the minister's immigration responsibilities take up much of his time. One may rest assured that he cannot therefore deal satisfactorily with all the additional programs for which he is responsible. If the programs announced tonight are to be successful, I suggest that responsibility should be shared by another minister. Perhaps his parliamentary secretary could help. I submit, again, that it is not possible for the minister who has been given responsibility for these programs to do a satisfactory job with regard to them, and his failure will dishearten the people of Canada who expect good results.
Some hon. members have said that regional committees will be established under the Department of Manpower and Immigration. We have seen such regional committees throughout Canada and have noted that some regions received tremendous benefits whereas others received practically nothing. There ought to be an equal distribution of the benefits of this whole program. It is not good enough having a job acceleration program in one part of the country if you completely forget about the rest of the country. I am sure that all hon. members are aware of this problem. Unless the government corrects what is wrong, 24319-64
The Canadian Economy
such programs will do more to disunite this country than almost anything else.
We heard the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) speak of the various programs for which he is responsible. I give him full credit for some excellent legislation that is now before the House, or will be before us, touching labour problems. At the same time, I draw to his attention a situation involving Canadian Pacific Railway. It has been suggested that the Canadian Pacific will be cutting back on certain facilities. As of today there is to be a cut-back with regard to 25 porters and a reduction of between 20 and 25 dining cars. The company also is to reduce the size of the transcontinental "Canadian." There will be two sleeping cars operating between Vancouver and Montreal and Vancouver and Toronto.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 THE CANADIAN ECONOMY MEASURES TO INCREASE EMPLOYMENT AND PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext:
Not long ago we were under the impression that we were adopting a new transportation policy. The head of the Canadian Transport Commission is only concerned about economics and not about service to the public. We thought the commission had decided that there would be adequate main line passenger service, but we are now advised that this service will consist of about eight cars operating on the Vancouver-Toronto-Montreal runs. The commission's decision will mean a loss of job opportunities. Before making that decision it ought to have undertaken research into the matter. It is not good enough to say that we will provide money for certain fields of transportation.
We are all concerned about STOL, or short take-off and landing aircraft. Yet when you talk to Europeans about STOL aircraft service between Ottawa and Montreal they say the idea is absolutely nuts. The United States, to use an example, is pouring millions of dollars into ground transportation facilities. I hope that any amounts we spend on transport will include moneys for research and development to make use of existing facilities. Think of the operation of a STOL aircraft carrying 12 people, and compare that with a transport operation utilizing present facilities. Many additional jobs could be provided under a suitable transport program. Whether that is asking too much, I do not know.
I wish to raise another area of concern. I am sorry that the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Andras) is not here at 2.40 in the morning to listen to me. I point out that our entire land assembly program is a complete shambles. The minister has many times suggested that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation adequately serves the needs of the country. How can he say that in light of the many applications for student housing coming from the universities and colleges of this country? Those applicants are told that no money is available for them. This type of building program could create a tremendous number of job opportunities.
If the minister is truly concerned about urban development and wishes to provide houses for as many people as possible, why is money not made available for land assembly and why is there not legislation that will provide for the expropriation of land now in the hands of land speculators? If the minister is concerned about these areas, he should do something. He should try to bring

The Canadian Economy
about co-operation that will enable citizens in the lower income brackets to avail themselves of some of our land.
We can talk all we want about creating jobs. This is one of the main purposes of the program. Some members have said that we should not criticize the 7 per cent and the 3 per cent. This is one of the areas where people who have it will get more, and those who do not have it will end up with less. The shots are being called outside this country. Makeshift policies are being developed with regard to Japan and Russia, among other countries. Makeshift policies will not work in this country unless we are able to call the shots. If the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is not prepared to indicate to the House what he intends to do in this other area, these makeshift job opportunities will not be successful. The whole thing
hinges on the fact that the shots must be called in Canada. You cannot call the shot in one area and expect any real development in another.
We hope some of the provisions and suggestions made tonight by the Minister of Finance will have a rub-off effect. There must be meaningful planning on a regional basis. All the talk and rhetoric we heard tonight will do nothing to strengthen the economy of this country.
